rulings.reason: The instruction scores only the presence of layout devices -- headings, numbering, an executive summary -- and never asks whether the labeled points contain any argument, so a comment could earn 10 for formatting an empty list. It is a document-preparation marker of professional drafting, which plausibly co-occurs with better substance but is not itself evidence about it.

The headline instruction asks whether the text 'was written for this proposal by this writer' and its discriminating low anchors key on campaign language, stock framings, and signature blocks revealing a mass-submission channel -- a fingerprint of who produced the comment and through what pipeline, which is the Track-B definition. The 10-vs-6 split does reach real content specificity, so individually composed comments plausibly carry genuinely better reasoning as well.

It scores genre and packaging -- salutation, docket/RIN caption, identifying closing -- and the proposer's own example (R59) is conceded to have substantive technical content while scoring 0, which shows the criterion cuts across substance rather than tracking it. Formal captioning correlates with experienced institutional submitters who may also argue better, so it is mixed.

The instruction explicitly directs the judge to 'score the question, not the precision,' so the score is set by which issue the docket put in front of the commenter rather than by anything the commenter did well -- a stakes/topic marker in the Track-B sense. Engaging a genuinely contested question does invite deeper analysis, so the underlying cause plausibly produces real quality too.
